c-lang.title: 01. Difference between `const int *p`, `int * const p`, and `const int * const p`
c-lang.content: `const int *p` is a mutable pointer to constant data, `int * const p` is a constant pointer to mutable data, and `const int * const p` locks both.

blocks.text:
• Reading right-to-left around `*`:
  - `const int *p` (same as `int const *p`): `p` is a pointer to a `const int`. You can reassign `p = &y`, but cannot modify `*p = 5`.
  - `int * const p`: `p` is a `const` pointer to `int`. You can modify `*p = 5`, but cannot reassign `p = &y` (must be initialized at declaration).
  - `const int * const p`: Neither `p` nor `*p` can be modified through `p`.

c-lang.title: 02. How does Pointer Arithmetic work (`ptr + 1`) across different types?
c-lang.content: Adding `n` to a pointer `T *ptr` advances its byte address by `n * sizeof(T)`, and subtracting two pointers of the same array yields the element count (`ptrdiff_t`).

blocks.text:
• Scaling rule: If `int *p` is at `0x1000` (`sizeof(int) == 4`), then `p + 1` is `0x1004`, whereas `char *c` at `0x1000` gives `c + 1 == 0x1001`.
• `void *` arithmetic: Illegal in standard C because `void` has no size (GCC allows it as a 1-byte extension—avoid for portability).
• Pointer subtraction: `p2 - p1` divides the byte difference by `sizeof(T)` and is only valid within the same array (or one-past-the-end).

c-lang.title: 03. Compare Dangling, Wild, and NULL Pointers (and Use-After-Free)
c-lang.content: A wild pointer is uninitialized garbage, a dangling pointer points to freed or out-of-scope memory, and `NULL` represents an explicit invalid sentinel.

blocks.text:
• Wild pointer: `int *p;` (uninitialized local)—contains indeterminate stack garbage; dereferencing is immediate UB.
• Dangling pointer: Points to heap memory already passed to `free(p)` (Use-After-Free) or a popped stack frame.
• Mitigation: Always initialize pointers (`= NULL`), set `p = NULL` after `free(p)` where practical, and compile with `-fsanitize=address` in testing.

c-lang.title: 04. What is the difference between `.data`, `.bss`, and `.rodata` segments?
c-lang.content: `.data` stores non-zero initialized globals/statics inside the binary file, `.bss` records only the size of zero-initialized globals/statics (saving disk space), and `.rodata` holds read-only literals.

blocks.text:
• `.data` vs `.bss`: Declaring `int big[1000000];` (uninitialized) puts it in `.bss`—it adds 0 bytes to the ELF binary on disk! Declaring `int big[1000000] = {1};` puts 4MB into `.data` inside the executable.
• `.rodata` trap: Modifying a string literal (`char *s = "abc"; s[0] = 'x';`) triggers a Segmentation Fault because `.rodata` is mapped read-only (use `char s[] = "abc";` to copy onto the stack).

blocks.code:
char *ro = "hello";   // Points to .rodata -> ro[0] = 'H' is UB / SIGSEGV
char rw[] = "hello";  // Array on stack initialized from literal -> rw[0] = 'H' is safe

c-lang.title: 05. Compare Stack vs Heap Allocation and explain Stack Overflow vs Heap Fragmentation
c-lang.content: Stack allocation is O(1) pointer movement with automatic LIFO lifetime and small fixed limits (~1-8MB), while Heap allocation is flexible and long-lived but slower and prone to leaks/fragmentation.

blocks.text:
• Stack: Deterministic LIFO cleanup, CPU-cache hot, fast (just moves `RSP`), but limited size (e.g., 8MB on Linux). Deep recursion or huge local arrays (`int buf[10000000]`) cause Stack Overflow.
• Heap: Explicit lifetime (`malloc`/`free`), supports large or runtime-sized buffers, but requires allocator metadata, thread synchronization, and manual cleanup.

c-lang.title: 06. Compare `malloc`, `calloc`, `realloc`, and `free` (including common pitfalls)
c-lang.content: `malloc` returns uninitialized bytes, `calloc(n, sz)` zero-initializes and guards against multiplication overflow, and `realloc` may move the block—always assign `realloc` to a temporary pointer.

blocks.text:
• `malloc(size)`: Leaves memory uninitialized (garbage).
• `calloc(count, size)`: Zeroes all allocated bytes and checks `count * size` overflow.
• `realloc(ptr, new_size)` trap: If `realloc` fails and returns `NULL`, overwriting `ptr = realloc(ptr, ...)` leaks the original block! Always use a temp pointer.
• `free(NULL)`: Guaranteed safe no-op by the C standard.

c-lang.title: 07. Explain the different meanings of the `static` keyword in C
c-lang.content: `static` gives local variables static storage duration (persisting across calls), gives file-scope globals/functions internal linkage (private to the `.c` file), and in C99 marks minimum array parameter sizes.

blocks.text:
• 1. Inside a function (`static int count = 0;`): Stored in `.data`/`.bss` instead of the stack; initialized once and retains its value across calls.
• 2. At file scope (`static void helper(void)` / `static int state;`): Internal linkage—invisible to other translation units (`.c` files), preventing symbol clashes.
• 3. C99 array parameters (`void f(int arr[static 10])`): Guarantees `arr` is non-NULL and points to at least 10 `int`s.

c-lang.title: 08. Difference between Declaration and Definition (`extern`), and avoiding Multiple Definition errors
c-lang.content: A declaration announces a symbol's type (`extern int g_val;`) without allocating storage, while a definition allocates storage (`int g_val = 0;`); put `extern` declarations in `.h` and definitions in one `.c` file.

blocks.text:
• Trap: Writing `int g_count = 0;` in a header `.h` included by two `.c` files causes a linker `multiple definition of 'g_count'` error!
• Correct pattern: Put `extern int g_count;` in `state.h` and `int g_count = 0;` in `state.c`.
• Note on functions: Function prototypes are implicitly `extern` by default unless marked `static`.

c-lang.title: 09. Compare `sizeof` vs `strlen`, and what happens in `sizeof(x++)`?
c-lang.content: `sizeof` is a compile-time operator returning byte size (does NOT evaluate its operand except for VLAs), whereas `strlen` scans memory at runtime until `'\0'`.

blocks.text:
• `sizeof("hello")`: Returns `6` (includes null terminator `'\0'`). `strlen("hello")`: Returns `5`.
• Pointer trap: For `const char *s = "hello";`, `sizeof(s)` is `8` (pointer size on 64-bit), NOT `6`.
• Unevaluated operand: `int x = 5; size_t sz = sizeof(x++);` leaves `x == 5` because `sizeof` inspects only the type at compile time.

c-lang.title: 10. Why are `gets`, `strcpy`, and `sprintf` dangerous, and how do you handle C strings safely?
c-lang.content: Unbounded string functions ignore destination buffer sizes and cause stack/heap buffer overflows; use `fgets`, `snprintf`, and `strncpy` pitfalls-aware bounded copies.

blocks.text:
• `gets()`: Removed in C11 because it cannot limit input length.
• `strncpy()` trap: Does NOT guarantee null-termination if `src` >= `n`! Always enforce `dst[n - 1] = '\0'` or use `snprintf(dst, sizeof(dst), "%s", src)` (which always null-terminates when `size > 0` and reports truncation via return value >= `sizeof(dst)`).

c-lang.title: 11. How do you Set, Clear, Toggle, and Test bits using Bitwise Operators in C?
c-lang.content: Use `|= (1U << k)` to set, `&= ~(1U << k)` to clear, `^= (1U << k)` to toggle, and `(x >> k) & 1U` to test bit `k`—always using `1U` to avoid signed shift UB.

blocks.text:
• Always use unsigned `1U << k` (or `UINT32_C(1) << k`): Shifting `1` into the sign bit of a 32-bit signed `int` (`1 << 31`) is Undefined Behavior in C!
• Operations:
  - Set bit `k`: `flags |= (1U << k);`
  - Clear bit `k`: `flags &= ~(1U << k);`
  - Toggle bit `k`: `flags ^= (1U << k);`
  - Test bit `k`: `bool is_set = (flags & (1U << k)) != 0;`

blocks.code:
#define BIT(k) (1U << (k))
uint32_t reg = 0;
reg |= BIT(3);   // Set bit 3
reg &= ~BIT(3);  // Clear bit 3
reg ^= BIT(2);   // Toggle bit 2

c-lang.title: 12. Walk through the 4 stages of the C Compilation Pipeline
c-lang.content: C source builds through Preprocessing (`.i`), Compilation to Assembly (`.s`), Assembly to Object code (`.o`), and Linking into an executable or library.

blocks.text:
• 1. Preprocessor (`gcc -E`): Expands `#include`, `#define` macros, `#ifdef` conditionals, and removes comments -> `.i`.
• 2. Compiler (`gcc -S`): Parses, type-checks, optimizes, and emits target assembly -> `.s`.
• 3. Assembler (`gcc -c`): Converts assembly into machine-code relocatable object files -> `.o` (unresolved external symbols remain).
• 4. Linker (`ld`): Combines `.o` files and libraries, resolves external symbols, and assigns final virtual addresses.

c-lang.title: 13. Why do C headers need Include Guards (`#ifndef`), and how do Forward Declarations speed up builds?
c-lang.content: Include guards prevent duplicate type definitions when a header is included transitively multiple times; forward declarations (`struct Node;`) break header cycles and reduce recompile cascades.

blocks.text:
• `#ifndef FOO_H / #define FOO_H / #endif`: Strictly portable C standard guard against multiple inclusion within one translation unit (`#pragma once` is widely supported but non-standard and can fail on symlinked paths).
• Forward declarations: If a header only uses pointers (`struct Context *`), write `struct Context;` instead of `#include "context.h"` to break circular dependencies and speed up incremental builds.

blocks.code:
#ifndef BUFFER_H
#define BUFFER_H
struct Allocator; // Forward declaration avoids pulling allocator.h
typedef struct Buffer Buffer;
#endif

c-lang.title: 14. Why is returning a pointer to a local variable UB, while returning a `struct` by value works?
c-lang.content: A local variable's stack storage ends when the function returns (leaving a dangling pointer), whereas returning a `struct` by value copies its contents to the caller's frame or registers.

blocks.text:
• Pointer to local: `int *f(void) { int x = 5; return &x; }` returns the address of a popped stack frame—subsequent calls overwrite it.
• Returning a `struct`: Small structs return in CPU registers (x86-64 SysV ABI returns structs <= 16 bytes in `RAX`/`RDX`), and larger structs use a hidden caller-allocated pointer (RVO-like ABI copy).

c-lang.title: 15. Why prefer `enum` over `#define` for integer constants in C?
c-lang.content: `enum` constants respect scope, survive preprocessing into debugger symbol tables (GDB/LLDB), group related values cleanly, and allow compiler `-Wswitch` exhaustiveness warnings.

blocks.text:
• `#define`: Blind text substitution before compilation—no debugger symbol names, no scope.
• `enum`: Compiler assigns sequential integers, preserves symbolic names in debuggers, and warns on missing `switch` cases (`-Wswitch`).
• Limitation: In C (prior to C23 fixed underlying types `enum E : uint8_t`), `enum` constants have type `int`.

c-lang.title: 16. Explain Array-to-Pointer Decay (`sizeof(arr)` vs `sizeof(&arr[0])`) and `&arr`
c-lang.content: In most expressions an array `T arr[N]` decays to `T *` pointing to `arr[0]`, EXCEPT as the operand of `sizeof`, `_Alignof`, or unary `&` (`&arr` has type `T (*)[N]`).

blocks.text:
• Exceptions to decay: `sizeof(arr)` gives total array bytes (`N * sizeof(T)`), whereas passing `arr` to a function decays it to a pointer (`sizeof(param)` inside the function equals `sizeof(void*)`!).
• `&arr` vs `arr`: Both evaluate to the same starting address, but `arr + 1` advances by `sizeof(T)` while `&arr + 1` advances by the ENTIRE array size (`N * sizeof(T)`).

blocks.code:
int arr[5] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
printf("%zu\n", sizeof(arr)); // 20 (5 * 4 bytes)
int *p = arr;                 // Decays to int *
printf("%zu\n", sizeof(p));   // 8 on 64-bit
int (*pa)[5] = &arr;          // Pointer to whole array of 5 ints

c-lang.title: 17. What is a `void *` pointer, and how is it used for Generic Programming in C?
c-lang.content: `void *` is an untyped generic data pointer that converts implicitly to/from any object pointer; it cannot be dereferenced directly without casting to a concrete type.

blocks.text:
• Properties: Holds any object address (`malloc` returns `void *`, `qsort` / `pthread_create` accept `void *`).
• Restrictions: Cannot dereference `*vp` or perform standard pointer arithmetic directly because the pointed-to size is unknown.
• Portability warning: Function pointers (`int (*)(int)`) are NOT guaranteed by the C standard to convert cleanly to/from `void *` (though POSIX `dlsym` relies on it).

c-lang.title: 18. How do Function Pointers work, and how do you read complex declarations?
c-lang.content: A function pointer stores the entry address of executable code in the `.text` segment, enabling callbacks, dispatch jump tables, and runtime polymorphism; `typedef` keeps complex signatures readable.

blocks.text:
• Right-Left / Spiral Rule: `int (*(*fn)(int))[5]` reads as: `fn` is a pointer to a function taking `int`, returning a pointer to an array of 5 `int`s.
• Best practice: Always `typedef` function pointer types (`typedef int (*Handler)(const char *);`) for clean APIs and dispatch tables.

c-lang.title: 19. When do you use a Pointer to a Pointer (`int **`) in C?
c-lang.content: Use `T **` when a function needs to rebind a caller's pointer (pass-by-reference for pointers), represent a ragged array of strings (`char **argv`), or allocate dynamic 2D arrays.

blocks.text:
• Pass-by-value trap: C passes everything by value, including pointers! Modifying `p = malloc(...)` inside `void alloc(int *p)` only mutates the local copy.
• Fix: Pass `&ptr` to `void alloc(int **p)` so `*p = malloc(...)` updates the caller's pointer.
• Linked lists: Using `Node **curr` (Linus Torvalds' 'good taste' trick) eliminates head special-cases when deleting nodes.

c-lang.title: 20. Describe the Memory Layout of a Running C Program
c-lang.content: A C process virtual address space consists of Text (code), Initialized Data (`.data`), Uninitialized Data (`.bss`), Heap (grows upward), and Stack (grows downward).

blocks.text:
• Segments from low to high virtual addresses:
  1. Text (`.text`): Compiled machine instructions (read-only, executable, shareable across processes).
  2. `.rodata`: Read-only constants and string literals (`"hello"`).
  3. `.data`: Explicitly initialized globals and `static` variables.
  4. `.bss`: Uninitialized / zero-initialized globals and `static` variables (zeroed by OS at load time).
  5. Heap: Dynamic allocations (`malloc`/`free`), grows toward higher addresses (`brk`/`mmap`).
  6. Stack: Function call frames, locals, return addresses, grows downward.

blocks.code:
int g_init = 5;       // .data
int g_zero;           // .bss
const char *s = "hi"; // s in .data, "hi" in .rodata
void f(void) { int local = 1; int *h = malloc(4); } // local on Stack, *h on Heap

c-lang.title: 21. How do Memory Leaks and Double Frees happen, and what tools catch them?
c-lang.content: Memory leaks occur when heap pointers are lost without `free()`; double free corrupts allocator metadata (and is an exploitable vulnerability); AddressSanitizer and Valgrind detect both.

blocks.text:
• Leak patterns: Early `return` on error paths before `free()`, overwriting a pointer before freeing, or failing to free nested struct fields.
• Double free: Calling `free(p)` twice corrupts freelist pointers (tcache/fastbin attacks) and triggers UB/aborts.
• Tooling: Compile with `-fsanitize=address,undefined -g` (ASan + UBSan) in CI/dev, or run under `valgrind --leak-check=full`.

c-lang.title: 22. Why does the compiler add Padding to Structs, and how do you minimize `sizeof(struct)`?
c-lang.content: Compilers insert padding bytes so each member sits at an address divisible by its natural alignment and total struct size is a multiple of its largest alignment; order members largest-to-smallest to minimize waste.

blocks.text:
• Hardware reason: CPUs read aligned 4/8-byte words in a single bus cycle; unaligned reads incur multi-cycle penalties or hardware faults (ARM/RISC-V).
• Rules:
  1. Each member offset must be a multiple of its alignment (`alignof(member)`).
  2. Total `sizeof(struct)` is padded to a multiple of the strictest member alignment (so arrays of structs stay aligned!).
• Optimization: Sort fields from largest alignment to smallest (`double`/`void*` -> `int` -> `short` -> `char`).

blocks.code:
struct Bad  { char a; int b; char c; }; // 1 + (3 pad) + 4 + 1 + (3 pad) = 12 bytes
struct Good { int b; char a; char c; }; // 4 + 1 + 1 + (2 pad) = 8 bytes

c-lang.title: 23. How do `union`s work in C, and what is a Tagged Union?
c-lang.content: All members of a `union` share the same starting memory address (`sizeof` >= largest member), saving RAM for mutually exclusive variants when paired with a discriminant `enum` tag.

blocks.text:
• Memory sharing: Writing `u.f = 1.0f` overwrites the bytes of `u.i`.
• Tagged Union pattern: Wrap an `enum Tag` + `union` inside a `struct` so code always knows which field is currently active.
• Type punning note: Reading an inactive union member is allowed in C99/C11 (unlike C++ where it is UB!), though `memcpy` remains the clearest, portable type-punning idiom.

c-lang.title: 24. What does `volatile` do in C, and why is it NOT sufficient for multithreading?
c-lang.content: `volatile` stops the compiler from caching or eliding loads/stores because the memory can change externally (MMIO, ISRs), but it provides NO atomicity or CPU memory-ordering barriers for threads.

blocks.text:
• What `volatile` prevents: Dead-store elimination, hoisting reads out of `while (*reg == 0)` loops, and reordering accesses relative to other `volatile` accesses.
• Valid uses: Memory-Mapped I/O (hardware registers), globals modified by Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs), and locals preserved across `setjmp`/`longjmp`.
• Why NOT for threads: `volatile int x; x++;` is still a non-atomic read-modify-write race, and CPUs/compilers can reorder non-volatile memory around it—use `<stdatomic.h>` or mutexes.

c-lang.title: 25. Can a variable be both `const` and `volatile`? Give a real-world example.
c-lang.content: Yes — `const volatile` means your code cannot write to the object (`const`), while external hardware or an ISR can change its value at any time (`volatile`).

blocks.text:
• Meaning: `const` is a compile-time contract enforced on *your code* ('read-only by software'), whereas `volatile` tells the optimizer ('value may change outside normal control flow').
• Classic example: A hardware timer tick counter or read-only device status register mapped into memory—software must only read it, and every read must fetch the fresh hardware state.

c-lang.title: 26. Distinguish Undefined Behavior (UB), Implementation-Defined, and Unspecified Behavior
c-lang.content: Implementation-defined behavior is documented by the compiler (`sizeof(int)`), unspecified behavior picks among valid options without documentation (arg eval order), and UB imposes zero requirements.

blocks.text:
• Implementation-defined: Compiler/target must choose and document it (e.g., `sizeof(long)`, signedness of `char`, right-shift of negative signed int in practice).
• Unspecified: Standard allows multiple valid choices (e.g., evaluation order of `f() + g()`).
• Undefined Behavior (UB): Anything can happen—crash, silent corruption, or compiler deleting security checks because optimizers assume UB never occurs!

c-lang.title: 27. Why is `i = i++ + ++i;` Undefined Behavior? (Sequence Points / Sequencing Rules)
c-lang.content: Modifying a scalar object more than once—or reading and modifying it without sequencing—between two sequence points is Undefined Behavior.

blocks.text:
• Sequencing rule: In `i++ + ++i` or `a[i] = i++`, the side effects on `i` and value computations are unsequenced relative to each other.
• Sequence points exist at `;`, `&&`, `||`, `?:`, `,` (comma operator, NOT function argument commas!), and after evaluating function arguments before entering the call.
• Fix: Split increments into separate statements.

c-lang.title: 28. Difference between `memcpy` and `memmove`, and how is `memmove` implemented?
c-lang.content: `memcpy` assumes non-overlapping regions (overlapping is UB) for maximum SIMD speed, whereas `memmove` checks overlap direction and copies backward when `dst > src`.

blocks.text:
• `memcpy(dst, src, n)`: Undefined Behavior if `[dst, dst+n)` overlaps `[src, src+n)`.
• `memmove(dst, src, n)`: Safe on overlapping buffers.
• Overlap logic: If `dst > src && dst < src + n`, copying forward would overwrite unread `src` bytes—so `memmove` copies backward from `n - 1` down to `0`.

c-lang.title: 29. Bitwise Tricks: Check Power of 2, Align Up to Alignment, and Detect Endianness
c-lang.content: `n && !(n & (n - 1))` tests powers of two, `(x + align - 1) & ~(align - 1)` rounds up to power-of-two alignment, and inspecting byte 0 of `uint32_t x = 1` reveals endianness.

blocks.text:
• Power of 2: `n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0` (must guard `n != 0`).
• Align up (when `align` is power of 2, e.g., 16): `(size + (align - 1)) & ~(align - 1)`.
• Endianness: Little-endian stores LSB at lowest address (`*(uint8_t *)&val == 1` for `uint32_t val = 1`); network byte order (TCP/IP) is Big-Endian (`htonl`/`ntohl`).

c-lang.title: 30. What are C Bitfields, and why should you be careful using them for binary protocols?
c-lang.content: Bitfields pack sub-byte integer members inside structs, but bit order (MSB-first vs LSB-first), padding, and plain `int` signedness are implementation-defined across compilers and architectures.

blocks.text:
• Portability pitfalls: The C standard leaves bit ordering within an allocation unit, crossing storage-unit boundaries, and whether `int flag : 1` is signed (`0` or `-1`!) up to the compiler/ABI.
• Best practice: Use explicit `unsigned int` for internal space-saving flags, and use explicit bitwise shifts/masks on `uint8_t`/`uint32_t` for portable wire/hardware formats.

c-lang.title: 31. Compare Static Linking (`.a`) vs Dynamic Linking (`.so` / `.dll`)
c-lang.content: Static linking embeds library code into the executable at build time (standalone, larger binary), while dynamic linking resolves shared `.so`/`.dll` libraries at load/run time (smaller binary, shared RAM pages).

blocks.text:
• Static library (`.a`, `ar rcs`): Linker copies only referenced `.o` members into the binary. Zero runtime dependency, slightly faster direct calls, but patching the library requires relinking.
• Dynamic/Shared library (`.so`, compiled with `-fPIC -shared`): Loaded by `ld.so` at startup (or `dlopen()` at runtime). Multiple processes share the `.text` RAM pages, and bugfixes drop in via library replacement (watch ABI compatibility!).

c-lang.title: 32. What are the classic C Macro Pitfalls, and why use `do { ... } while (0)`?
c-lang.content: Function-like macros suffer from operator precedence bugs, double evaluation of side-effect arguments (`MAX(i++, j++)`), and `if/else` dangling-semicolon breakage fixed by `do { ... } while(0)`.

blocks.text:
• Precedence trap: `#define SQ(x) x * x` turns `SQ(1 + 2)` into `1 + 2 * 1 + 2 == 5`! Always parenthesize parameters AND the whole expression: `((x) * (x))`.
• Double evaluation: `MAX(a++, b)` increments `a` twice! Prefer `static inline` functions.
• `do { ... } while (0)`: Wraps multi-statement macros into a single safe statement that consumes the caller's trailing `;` cleanly inside unbraced `if (...) MACRO(); else ...`.

blocks.code:
#define LOG_ERR(msg) do { \
    fprintf(stderr, "ERR: %s\n", (msg)); \
    err_count++; \
} while (0)

c-lang.title: 33. What is a Data Race in C11, and how do Mutexes (`pthread_mutex_t`) prevent it?
c-lang.content: In C11, concurrent unsynchronized access to the same memory location where at least one access is a write is a Data Race (Undefined Behavior); mutexes enforce mutual exclusion and memory visibility.

blocks.text:
• Data Race = UB: Even on architectures with word-sized loads, the compiler can hoist or tear non-atomic reads/writes across threads unless synchronized.
• `pthread_mutex_t`: Guarantees only one thread enters the critical section at a time AND establishes a happens-before memory barrier between unlock and subsequent lock.

c-lang.title: 34. What causes Deadlocks in multithreaded C, and how do you prevent them?
c-lang.content: Deadlock occurs when threads hold locks while waiting in a cycle for each other's locks (Mutual Exclusion, Hold-and-Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait); break it via canonical lock ordering.

blocks.text:
• Classic ABBA deadlock: Thread 1 locks `A` then waits for `B`; Thread 2 locks `B` then waits for `A`.
• Preventions:
  1. Global Lock Ordering: Always acquire multiple locks in a fixed order (e.g., by ascending pointer address or ID).
  2. `pthread_mutex_trylock()` with backoff: Release held locks if the second cannot be acquired.
  3. Keep critical sections tiny and never call unknown user callbacks while holding a mutex.

c-lang.title: 35. Explain `fork()`, Copy-on-Write, `exec()`, and Zombie vs Orphan Processes
c-lang.content: `fork()` clones a process lazily via Copy-on-Write pages, `exec()` replaces the address space with a new program, and un-waited exited children become Zombies until the parent calls `waitpid()`.

blocks.text:
• `fork()`: Returns `0` in the child and child PID in the parent; memory pages are shared read-only via Copy-on-Write until either writes.
• Zombie process: Child has exited, but its exit status sits in the kernel process table because parent hasn't called `wait()`/`waitpid()`.
• Orphan process: Parent exited first; child is re-parented to PID 1 (`init`/subreaper) which reaps it.

c-lang.title: 36. Why are Variable-Length Arrays (VLAs) and `alloca()` risky in production C?
c-lang.content: VLAs and `alloca()` allocate dynamic sizes on the stack without returning `NULL` on failure; an oversized input silently causes Stack Overflow or security vulnerabilities.

blocks.text:
• Risk: `int buf[n];` where `n` comes from untrusted input or exceeds stack space crashes immediately (or jumps past the guard page!). Unlike `malloc()`, VLAs have no error return.
• Standard status: C11 downgraded VLAs to an optional feature (`__STDC_NO_VLA__`); Linux kernel banned VLAs (`-Wvla`).
• Alternative: Fixed-size stack buffer for bounded small `n` or `malloc` + `free`.

c-lang.title: 37. How do Variadic Functions (`<stdarg.h>`) work, and what are Format String Vulnerabilities?
c-lang.content: Variadic functions (`...`) walk extra arguments via `va_list`, `va_start`, `va_arg`, and `va_end`; passing untrusted input directly as the format string to `printf(user_str)` allows arbitrary memory read/write.

blocks.text:
• `<stdarg.h>` rules: Always pair `va_start(ap, last_named)` with `va_end(ap)`. Default argument promotions apply: `float` promotes to `double`, and `char`/`short` promote to `int`.
• Format string attack: `printf(user_input)` lets an attacker pass `%x.%x.%s.%n` to leak stack memory or write arbitrary values via `%n`! Always write `printf("%s", user_input)`.

c-lang.title: 38. How do ELF Sections (`.text`, `.rodata`, `.data`, `.bss`) map to Program Header Segments (`PT_LOAD`) at runtime?
c-lang.content: Linkers use ELF Section Headers for symbol resolution and relocation at build time, while the OS kernel's ELF loader ignores sections and maps grouped Program Header segments (`PT_LOAD`) directly into virtual memory pages with hardware R/W/X permissions.

blocks.text:
• **Linking View vs Execution View**: Section headers (`.text`, `.rodata`, `.data`, `.bss`, `.symtab`) organize code and data for the static linker (`ld`). At runtime, `execve()` only reads the **Program Header Table** (`PT_LOAD`, `PT_DYNAMIC`, `PT_INTERP`).
• **Page Permission Grouping**: The linker merges sections with identical memory permissions into single `PT_LOAD` segments aligned to 4KB page boundaries: `.text` fits into an `R-X` segment, `.rodata` into an `R--` segment, and `.data` + `.bss` into an `RW-` segment.
• **`.bss` Optimization**: In the ELF file on disk, `.bss` has `p_filesz < p_memsz`; the kernel zero-maps anonymous demand-zero pages for the difference without wasting disk bytes.

c-lang.title: 39. Why does the order of static libraries (`.a`) on the linker command line matter, and how does `--gc-sections` strip dead code?
c-lang.content: The Unix linker processes static archives (`.a`) left-to-right in a single pass, pulling in only `.o` members that resolve currently undefined symbols, while `-ffunction-sections -fdata-sections` combined with `-Wl,--gc-sections` drops unused functions within a translation unit.

blocks.text:
• **Single-Pass Archive Resolution**: The linker maintains a set of unresolved symbols $U$. When it scans `libA.a`, it extracts only object files from `libA.a` that define symbols currently in $U$. If `libB.a` placed earlier depends on `libA.a`, `libA.a` must follow `libB.a` on the command line (or be wrapped in `-Wl,--start-group ... -Wl,--end-group`).
• **Object-Level Granularity**: By default, if you call one function in `utils.o`, the linker pulls the entire `utils.o` (including all unused functions inside it).
• **Section Garbage Collection**: Compiling with `-ffunction-sections -fdata-sections` places each function/variable in its own `.text.func_name` section, allowing `-Wl,--gc-sections` to discard unreferenced functions.

c-lang.title: 40. When can a C compiler apply Tail-Call Optimization (TCO) to convert a `CALL` into a `JMP`, and what prevents it?
c-lang.content: TCO reuses the current stack frame and replaces `call + ret` with a direct `jmp` when a function's final action is returning the result of another call, provided no pointers to local stack variables escape and stack arguments don't exceed the caller's frame.

blocks.text:
• **How TCO Works**: Instead of pushing a new return address and growing the stack $O(N)$, the compiler pops its frame, places arguments in `RDI..R9`, and executes `jmp target` so the callee returns directly to the original caller ($O(1)$ stack space).
• **What Blocks TCO in C**:
  1. Passing the address of a local stack variable (`&local`) to the callee (the variable would vanish when the frame is reused!).
  2. Performing any computation after the call returns (e.g., `return n * fact(n - 1)` is NOT a tail call; needs an accumulator).
  3. Callee requiring more stack-passed arguments than the caller allocated.
• **Explicit Enforcement**: Clang/GCC 15+ support `__attribute__((musttail))` on `return` statements to guarantee TCO or fail compilation.

c-lang.title: 41. How did C11 replace 'Sequence Points' with 'Sequenced-Before' relations, and why is function argument evaluation order still trap-prone?
c-lang.content: C11 replaced global sequence points with a partial ordering graph ('sequenced-before', 'indeterminately sequenced', and 'unsequenced'); function arguments are unsequenced relative to each other, so mutating a variable in two arguments of the same call is UB, while calling two functions that mutate shared state is indeterminately sequenced.

blocks.text:
• **Three Ordering Relations (C11 §5.1.2.3)**:
  1. **Sequenced-before**: $A$ completes all value computations and side effects before $B$ begins (e.g., `&&`, `||`, `?:`, comma operator `,`, full expression `;`).
  2. **Indeterminately sequenced**: Either $A$ runs before $B$ or $B$ before $A$—they do NOT interleave (e.g., two function calls `f() + g()`).
  3. **Unsequenced**: Operations may overlap/interleave. An unsequenced side effect on a scalar object with another side effect or read of the same scalar is **Undefined Behavior**.
• **Classic Argument Trap**: In `printf("%d %d\n", ++i, ++i);`, the two `++i` expressions are unsequenced -> **UB**! In `f(get_next(), get_next())`, the two calls are indeterminately sequenced -> **Unspecified Behavior** (GCC on x86 often evaluates right-to-left, Clang left-to-right!).

c-lang.title: 42. What are the Undefined Behavior corner cases of bitwise shifts (`<<` and `>>`) in C, and how do you write a safe bit-rotate (`rotl32`)?
c-lang.content: Shifting by a negative count or by `>=` the promoted bit-width (e.g., `1U << 32`), or left-shifting a signed integer into/past the sign bit (`1 << 31`), is Undefined Behavior; naive `(x << n) | (x >> (32 - n))` triggers UB when `n == 0` unless masked with `(-n) & 31`.

blocks.text:
• **4 Bit-Shift UB Rules (C11 §6.5.7)**:
  1. Shift count `< 0` or `>= width` of the promoted left operand (e.g., `uint32_t x >> 32` is UB; on x86 `SHR` masks the shift register by `31`, turning `>> 32` into `>> 0` instead of `0`!).
  2. Left-shifting a negative value (`-1 << 2` is UB).
  3. Left-shifting a positive **signed** value into the sign bit (`1 << 31` is UB for 32-bit `int`; always use `1U << 31`).
  4. Right-shifting a negative signed value (`-4 >> 1`) is **Implementation-Defined** (arithmetic shift on most compilers, not UB).
• **Safe Branchless Rotate**: Naive `(x << n) | (x >> (32 - n))` shifts by `32` when `n == 0` (UB!). Masking `(x << (n & 31)) | (x >> ((-n) & 31))` avoids UB and compiles to a single `ROL` instruction!

c-lang.title: 43. How does `mmap()` perform Demand Paging and Zero-Copy file access via the kernel Page Cache?
c-lang.content: `mmap()` returns immediately after inserting a `vm_area_struct` (VMA) into the process's red-black/maple tree without allocating physical RAM or reading disk; pages are populated lazily on the first CPU access via minor/major page faults directly mapping the kernel Page Cache into user virtual space.

blocks.text:
• **Lazy VMA Creation**: Calling `mmap()` on a 10GB file completes in microseconds because zero bytes are read from disk and zero page-table entries (`PTE`s) are created upfront.
• **Minor vs Major Page Faults**:
  - **Major Fault**: First read of `[ptr + offset]` faults into the kernel; if the 4KB file block isn't in RAM, the kernel reads it from disk into the **Page Cache** and wires the process's `PTE` directly to that physical Page Cache frame (zero copy between kernel and user buffers!).
  - **Minor Fault**: The file page is already in the kernel Page Cache (or is an anonymous demand-zero page); the kernel just wires the `PTE` in nanoseconds with no disk I/O.
• **`MAP_SHARED` vs `MAP_PRIVATE`**: `MAP_SHARED` writes dirty the Page Cache directly (flushed asynchronously or via `msync()`); `MAP_PRIVATE` triggers a Copy-on-Write private page on the first write.

c-lang.title: 44. Explain `stdio` buffering modes (`_IOFBF`, `_IOLBF`, `_IONBF`) and why `printf()` before `fork()` prints twice when redirected to a file.
c-lang.content: `stdout` is line-buffered (`_IOLBF`) when attached to an interactive TTY (`isatty(1) == 1`) but switches to 4KB full-buffered (`_IOFBF`) when piped or redirected to a file; calling `fork()` with unflushed user-space `FILE` buffers clones the pending bytes into both parent and child, causing duplicate output on exit.

blocks.text:
• **Three `stdio` Modes (configured via `setvbuf`)**:
  - **`_IONBF` (Unbuffered)**: `stderr` default—every write immediately calls `write(2, ...)`. 
  - **`_IOLBF` (Line-Buffered)**: `stdout` default on a terminal—flushes to the kernel when `\n` is written or buffer fills.
  - **`_IOFBF` (Fully-Buffered)**: `stdout` default when redirected (`./app > out.log`)—accumulates 4KB/8KB inside the user-space `FILE` struct before calling `write()`.
• **The Classic `printf` + `fork()` Bug**: If you run `printf("Starting...");` (no `\n` or redirected to a file) and then call `fork()`, the string sits in `stdout`'s user-space heap buffer. `fork()` duplicates the user-space memory into the child, so when both parent and child call `exit()`, both flush their copy of `stdout`—printing `"Starting..."` twice! Fix: call `fflush(NULL)` before `fork()`.

c-lang.title: 45. How does the Opaque Pointer (Incomplete Type) pattern enforce encapsulation and preserve ABI compatibility in C shared libraries?
c-lang.content: Declaring `typedef struct Engine Engine;` in the public `.h` header while keeping `struct Engine { ... }` inside the private `.c` file prevents callers from stacking-allocating or accessing struct fields directly, allowing library updates to reorder or add fields without breaking binary ABI compatibility.

blocks.text:
• **Why Exposing Struct Definitions Breaks the ABI**: If a public header defines `struct Context { int a; int b; };`, client binaries hardcode `sizeof(struct Context) == 8` and field offsets (`offsetof == 4`) directly into their machine code. Adding a single field in v1.1 forces every downstream consumer to recompile or suffer memory corruption!
• **Opaque Pointer Pattern**:
  - Public header (`engine.h`): `typedef struct Engine Engine; Engine *engine_create(void); void engine_destroy(Engine *);`
  - Since all object pointers in C have the same size and representation (`8 bytes` on 64-bit), clients pass `Engine *` around without knowing its size or layout.

c-lang.title: 46. How do C11 `_Generic` type-generic expressions and `_Static_assert` enable compile-time polymorphism and invariants in C?
c-lang.content: `_Generic((expr), type1: val1, type2: val2, default: valN)` dispatches at compile time based on the un-evaluated type of `expr` (after array-to-pointer decay and qualifier stripping), while `_Static_assert(cond, msg)` enforces struct sizes, alignments, and ABI invariants during compilation.

blocks.text:
• **How `_Generic` Works**: Unlike preprocessor text substitution, `_Generic` operates in the compiler's type checker. The controlling expression is **never evaluated at runtime** (similar to `sizeof`), and only the matching association branch is selected—giving C zero-overhead compile-time function overloading (as used in `<tgmath.h>`).
• **`_Static_assert` (and C23 `static_assert`)**: Evaluates an integer constant expression at compile time. Essential in systems C to verify that a struct fits evenly in a 64-byte cache line (`sizeof(struct Packet) == 64`) or has no unexpected padding.

c-lang.title: 47. What is the storage duration and lifetime trap of C99 Compound Literals (`(struct Point){ .x = 1, .y = 2 }`)?
c-lang.content: A compound literal declared at file scope has static storage duration, whereas one inside a function has automatic storage duration tied to its innermost enclosing `{ ... }` block—making it Undefined Behavior to return or store its address after that block exits.

blocks.text:
• **Unnamed Lvalues**: Unlike a cast, `(struct Config){ .timeout = 30 }` creates an unnamed **lvalue** object in memory whose address you can take (`&(struct Config){ .timeout = 30 }`).
• **Block-Scoped Lifetime Trap**: If you write `int *p; if (cond) { p = (int[]){1, 2, 3}; }`, the compound literal array's lifetime ends at the closing brace `}` of the `if` statement—NOT at the end of the function! Dereferencing `p` after the `if` block is a stack Use-After-Scope bug (caught by `AddressSanitizer`).
• **C23 Storage-Class Specifiers**: C23 now allows `(static const int[]){1, 2, 3}` inside a function to explicitly give a compound literal static lifetime in `.rodata`.

c-lang.title: 48. How does the X-Macro preprocessor pattern keep enums, string lookup tables, and serialization functions synchronized at compile time?
c-lang.content: An X-Macro defines a list of items as calls to a higher-order macro parameter `X(id, name, ...)` and expands that list multiple times with different definitions of `X`, guaranteeing single-source-of-truth synchronization between `enum` definitions, string arrays, and switch handlers.

blocks.text:
• **The Problem X-Macros Solve**: Maintaining an `enum ErrorCode` and a parallel `const char *error_names[]` array by hand inevitably leads to out-of-sync bugs when someone adds an enum value in the middle.
• **How Higher-Order X-Macros Work**:
  1. Define a table macro `ERROR_LIST(X)` that takes a macro `X` as an argument and invokes `X(...)` for each row.
  2. Pass a macro that extracts the enum identifier to generate the `enum`.
  3. Pass a macro that stringifies (`#name`) or extracts the description to generate the `static const char *const` array using designated initializers `[ERR_##name] = msg`.

blocks.code:
#define STATUS_TABLE(X)                  \
    X(OK,        200, "Success")         \
    X(NOT_FOUND, 404, "Resource missing")\
    X(ERR_INTERNAL, 500, "Server fault")

#define AS_ENUM(id, code, msg) STATUS_##id,
enum Status { STATUS_TABLE(AS_ENUM) STATUS_COUNT };

#define AS_STR(id, code, msg) [STATUS_##id] = msg,
static const char *const status_messages[] = { STATUS_TABLE(AS_STR) };

c-lang.title: 49. How does `__attribute__((cleanup(fn)))` provide deterministic RAII resource management in C (as used extensively in systemd and the Linux kernel)?
c-lang.content: Supported by GCC and Clang, `__attribute__((cleanup(fn)))` registers a callback `void fn(T *var)` that the compiler automatically invokes with a pointer to the variable whenever it exits its lexical scope via any return path, `break`, or `goto`.

blocks.text:
• **Eliminating `goto cleanup;` Boilerplate**: Traditional C functions with 5 resource acquisitions require a fragile pyramid of `goto err_free_c; goto err_close_fd;`. With `cleanup`, the compiler emits the cleanup call automatically at every scope exit.
• **How the Callback Works**: The cleanup function receives a **pointer to the variable** (so for `char *buf`, the callback signature is `void free_str(char **p)`).
• **Important Caveat**: The variable MUST be initialized at declaration (e.g., `= NULL` or `= -1`) because if an early `return` happens before assignment, the cleanup function still runs on that variable! Also note: `longjmp()` and `exit()` bypass scope cleanup.

c-lang.title: 50. Why is `if (a + b < a)` broken for checking signed overflow in C, and how do `__builtin_add_overflow()` and C23 `<stdckdint.h>` work?
c-lang.content: Writing `if (a + b < a)` for signed `int` evaluates `a + b` first—triggering Undefined Behavior that allows the compiler to optimize the check to `if (b < 0)`; `__builtin_add_overflow(a, b, &res)` and C23 `ckd_add(&res, a, b)` perform the arithmetic with infinite precision and test the CPU's hardware Overflow Flag (`JO`) in a single instruction.

blocks.text:
• **Why Post-Hoc Signed Checks Fail**: Once `a + b` overflows a signed `int`, UB has already occurred! At `-O2`, GCC/Clang simplify `(a + b) < a` algebraically into `b < 0`, completely defeating your security check!
• **Why Pre-Condition Checks Are Tedious**: Checking `if (b > 0 && a > INT_MAX - b)` before adding works, but requires multiple branches and doesn't map cleanly to a single hardware `ADD + JO` instruction pair.
• **Compiler Intrinsics & C23 `<stdckdint.h>`**: `__builtin_mul_overflow(count, size, &total)` (standardized in C23 as `ckd_mul(&total, count, size)`) performs the operation without UB, stores the wrapped result, and returns `true` directly from the CPU's carry/overflow flag (`CF`/`OF`) if overflow occurred.

c-lang.title: 51. How does Link-Time Optimization (`-flto`) work under the hood to inline functions across separate `.c` translation units?
c-lang.content: With `-flto`, compiling a `.c` file emits compiler intermediate representation (GIMPLE/LLVM Bitcode) into the `.o` file instead of final machine assembly, enabling the linker plugin to merge the whole program's call graph, inline cross-file functions, propagate constants, and strip dead code across translation units.

blocks.text:
• **Traditional Separate Compilation Barrier**: Without LTO, when `main.c` calls `vec_dot()` defined in `math.c`, the compiler compiling `main.c` only sees the header prototype and MUST emit a `CALL` instruction—preventing inlining, constant folding, and loop fusion across `.c` files.
• **Fat vs Thin LTO**:
  - **Full/Monolithic LTO**: Merges all IR bitcode into a single giant module at link time (maximum optimization, slow single-threaded link time).
  - **ThinLTO (`-flto=thin`)**: Builds a compact global function summary index first, then spawns parallel worker threads that import only the hot cross-module functions needed for inlining—scaling to massive codebases with near-incremental link times.

c-lang.title: 52. What does the `restrict` keyword (C99) guarantee to the compiler?
c-lang.content: `restrict` promises the compiler that for the lifetime of that pointer, no other pointer will access the same underlying memory, enabling vectorization and register caching.

blocks.text:
• Pointer aliasing problem: In `void add(int *a, int *b, int *c)`, the compiler must reload `*b` and `*c` on every loop iteration in case `a` aliases `b` or `c`.
• `restrict` contract: Tells the optimizer the regions do not overlap (e.g., `memcpy(void * restrict dst, const void * restrict src, size_t n)`). Violating `restrict` by passing overlapping pointers is Undefined Behavior!

c-lang.title: 53. Explain `offsetof()`, `__attribute__((packed))`, and C11 `alignas` / `alignof`
c-lang.content: `offsetof(T, member)` computes byte offsets portably, `packed` removes padding (at the risk of unaligned access), and C11 `<stdalign.h>` provides standard `alignas`/`alignof`.

blocks.text:
• `offsetof(type, member)` (`<stddef.h>`): Used heavily in kernel-style `container_of()` macros to recover a parent struct pointer from an embedded list node.
• `__attribute__((packed))` / `#pragma pack(1)`: Removes padding for wire/disk formats, but taking `&s.field` can produce an unaligned pointer causing UB or bus errors—prefer `memcpy` deserialization for network protocols!
• C11 `alignas(64)`: Aligns structs to CPU cache lines (64 bytes) to prevent false sharing.

c-lang.title: 54. What is a Flexible Array Member (FAM) in C99, and why is it better than a pointer?
c-lang.content: A Flexible Array Member (`char data[];` as the last struct member) allows allocating header + variable-length payload in a single contiguous `malloc`, improving cache locality and halving `free()` calls.

blocks.text:
• Syntax: Last member of a struct with >=1 other named member is `T data[];` (do NOT use the pre-C99 `data[0]` or `data[1]` hacks, which trigger UB under bounds checks).
• Benefits: One `malloc(sizeof(Packet) + len)`, contiguous memory for CPU cache, single `free(pkt)`.
• Note: `sizeof(struct Packet)` excludes the flexible array member.

c-lang.title: 55. Why use `static inline` instead of plain `inline` in C header files?
c-lang.content: In C99/C11, plain `inline` in a header does not emit an external symbol if the compiler chooses NOT to inline it (causing linker `undefined reference` errors); `static inline` guarantees self-contained linkage.

blocks.text:
• C99 `inline` quirk (different from C++!): An `inline` definition without `extern` provides an 'inline definition' only—at `-O0` (unoptimized debug builds), the compiler calls the function out-of-line and the linker fails unless one `.c` file has an `extern inline` instantiation.
• `static inline` in `.h`: Gives each translation unit internal linkage; compiles cleanly at `-O0` and inlines away at `-O2`, replacing unsafe `#define` macros with type safety.

c-lang.title: 56. Why is Signed Integer Overflow Undefined Behavior in C, while Unsigned Overflow is Well-Defined?
c-lang.content: Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 2^N per the C standard, whereas signed integer overflow is UB—allowing compilers to optimize away `if (x + 1 < x)` overflow checks completely.

blocks.text:
• Unsigned wraparound: `UINT_MAX + 1u == 0u` is guaranteed.
• Signed overflow UB trap: Checking `if (x + 100 < x)` AFTER adding `x + 100` can be deleted by GCC/Clang at `-O2` because the optimizer assumes signed overflow never happens!
• Safe overflow check: Check BEFORE adding (`if (x > INT_MAX - 100)`) or use C23 `<stdckdint.h>` (`ckd_add`) / `__builtin_add_overflow`.

c-lang.title: 57. Explain the Strict Aliasing Rule and how to safely do Type Punning
c-lang.content: Strict aliasing forbids accessing an object through a pointer of an incompatible type (allowing register optimizations), with exceptions for `char*`/`unsigned char*` and compatible/signed variants; use `memcpy` for portable type punning.

blocks.text:
• Rule (C99/C11 6.5/7): Compilers assume `int *` and `float *` never alias the same address, so writes via `float *` may not reload cached `*int_ptr` reads.
• Allowed exceptions: `char`/`unsigned char` (can inspect raw bytes of anything), signed/unsigned counterparts, or union/struct containing the type.
• Best portable type-punning: `uint32_t bits; memcpy(&bits, &f, sizeof(bits));`—GCC/Clang optimize `memcpy` of 4 bytes into a single CPU register move with zero overhead and zero UB!

c-lang.title: 58. Explain Integer Promotions and the Signed-to-Unsigned Conversion Bug
c-lang.content: Small types (`char`, `short`) promote to `int` in expressions, and mixing `int` with `unsigned int` (or `size_t`) silently converts the negative signed value into a huge unsigned value.

blocks.text:
• Classic bug: `-1 < 1U` evaluates to `0` (`false`)! Why? Usual arithmetic conversions promote `-1` (`int`) to `unsigned int` (`UINT_MAX`), which is greater than `1U`.
• Common real-world bug: `int len = -1; if (len < sizeof(buf))` converts `-1` to `SIZE_MAX` (`false`), bypassing bounds checks!
• Defense: Enable `-Wall -Wextra -Wsign-compare`.

c-lang.title: 59. How do C11 `<stdatomic.h>` Atomics and Memory Ordering (`acquire`/`release`) work?
c-lang.content: C11 `_Atomic` variables provide lock-free atomic operations and explicit memory fences (`memory_order_acquire`/`release`) to prevent CPU and compiler instruction reordering across cores.

blocks.text:
• Default (`memory_order_seq_cst`): Sequential consistency—safest, strongest global order.
• Acquire/Release pairing: Producer writes payload then stores `atomic_store_explicit(&ready, true, memory_order_release)`; Consumer loads `atomic_load_explicit(&ready, memory_order_acquire)`—guaranteeing all producer writes before the release are visible after the acquire!
• `memory_order_relaxed`: Atomicity only, no ordering guarantees (good for pure stats counters).

c-lang.title: 60. Why must `pthread_cond_wait()` always be wrapped in a `while` loop, not an `if`?
c-lang.content: POSIX condition variables can experience spurious wakeups or stolen wakeups (another consumer grabs the item first), so re-checking the predicate in a `while` loop is mandatory.

blocks.text:
• How `pthread_cond_wait(&cond, &mtx)` works: Atomically unlocks `mtx` and puts the thread to sleep; upon wakeup, it re-acquires `mtx` before returning.
• Why `while (!predicate)`: (1) OS signals/futexes allow spurious wakeups without `pthread_cond_signal`; (2) Another thread may consume the condition between `signal()` and re-acquiring `mtx`.

c-lang.title: 61. What makes a POSIX Signal Handler safe? (`volatile sig_atomic_t` & Async-Signal-Safe)
c-lang.content: Inside a POSIX signal handler, only async-signal-safe functions may be called (NO `printf` or `malloc`), and shared flags should have type `volatile sig_atomic_t`.

blocks.text:
• Reentrancy hazard: If a signal interrupts `malloc()` or `printf()` while they hold internal libc locks, calling `malloc()`/`printf()` inside the handler deadlocks or corrupts the heap!
• Safe pattern: Set a `volatile sig_atomic_t stop_flag = 1;` (or write 1 byte to a self-pipe via `write()`, which IS async-signal-safe) and handle cleanup in the main loop.

c-lang.title: 62. Why can `memcmp(&s1, &s2, sizeof(s1))` fail even when two structs have identical fields?
c-lang.content: Padding bytes inside structs hold indeterminate garbage unless zero-initialized with `memset` or `{0}` (and floats have `-0.0` vs `+0.0` / NaN), so `memcmp` can report false inequality.

blocks.text:
• Padding trap: Assigning `s1.a = 'x'; s1.b = 1;` leaves padding bytes between `a` and `b` uninitialized! Even `memset(&s, 0, sizeof(s))` may not stay zeroed if structs are later copied member-by-member.
• Fix: Write an explicit field-by-field `struct_equal(const S *a, const S *b)` function (also handles `float` NaN/-0.0 and pointer deep equality).

c-lang.title: 63. How do `setjmp()` and `longjmp()` work, and why do non-`volatile` locals break across `longjmp`?
c-lang.content: `setjmp`/`longjmp` perform non-local stack unwinding for C error recovery, and any non-`volatile` local variable modified after `setjmp()` has an indeterminate value after `longjmp()`.

blocks.text:
• Mechanism: `setjmp(env)` saves CPU registers (PC, SP, callee-saved regs) and returns `0`; `longjmp(env, val)` restores them and makes `setjmp` appear to return `val`.
• Register restoration trap: If local variable `x` lived in a CPU register and was modified after `setjmp`, `longjmp` restores old register state—marking `x` `volatile` forces it onto the stack.
• Limitation: Never `longjmp` into a function that has already returned!

c-lang.title: 64. Explain CPU Cache Locality (AoS vs SoA) and False Sharing in Multithreaded C
c-lang.content: Contiguous Structure-of-Arrays (SoA) maximizes 64-byte cache-line utilization over AoS, while False Sharing degrades multithreaded speed when two threads mutate independent variables on the same cache line.

blocks.text:
• AoS vs SoA: Iterating `particles[i].x` in Array-of-Structs (`struct Particle { float x, y, z, mass, ...; }`) wastes cache bandwidth loading unused fields; Structure-of-Arrays (`float x[N], y[N];`) enables dense cache lines and SIMD.
• False Sharing: Even if Thread 1 writes `counters[0]` and Thread 2 writes `counters[1]`, if both sit on the same 64-byte cache line, MESI cache coherency bounces the line between cores!
• Fix: Pad or align per-thread data to `alignas(64)`.

c-lang.title: 65. How do the Procedure Linkage Table (`.plt`) and Global Offset Table (`.got.plt`) implement lazy symbol binding in dynamically linked C binaries?
c-lang.content: To keep `.text` read-only and Position-Independent (PIC), external library calls jump to a `.plt` stub that indirects through a writable `.got.plt` pointer, lazily invoking `ld-linux.so` on the first call and patching the GOT slot for direct subsequent jumps.

blocks.text:
• **Position-Independent Code (PIC)**: Shared libraries (`.so`) can be loaded at any virtual address. Instead of patching read-only `.text` instructions (which would break page sharing across processes), calls use RIP-relative jumps to the `.plt`.
• **First Call (Lazy Resolution)**: Calling `printf@plt` jumps to `*(GOT[n])`, which initially points back into the `.plt` stub that pushes the relocation index and calls `_dl_runtime_resolve` in the dynamic linker.
• **Subsequent Calls**: `_dl_runtime_resolve` looks up `printf` in `libc.so`, overwrites `GOT[n]` with the real address, and future calls jump through `GOT[n]` in a single indirect branch.

c-lang.title: 66. What is RELRO (Relocation Read-Only), and how do Partial RELRO and Full RELRO defend against GOT overwrite exploits?
c-lang.content: Partial RELRO reorders ELF sections so `.got` precedes `.data`/`.bss` and marks non-PLT GOT entries read-only, while Full RELRO (`-Wl,-z,relro,-z,now`) eagerly resolves all dynamic symbols at startup and marks the entire `.got.plt` read-only via `mprotect()`.

blocks.text:
• **The Attack (GOT Overwrite)**: With lazy binding, `.got.plt` must stay writable (`RW-`) throughout execution. An attacker with an arbitrary-write primitive (e.g., via format string or heap overflow) can overwrite `GOT[printf]` with `system()`.
• **Partial RELRO** (GCC default): Places internal `.got` before `.bss` (so BSS buffer overflows cannot reach the GOT) and locks `.got` read-only, but leaves `.got.plt` writable for lazy binding.
• **Full RELRO**: Forces the dynamic linker to resolve every symbol before `main()` runs (`RTLD_NOW`) and changes `.got.plt` pages to `PROT_READ`, completely neutralizing GOT overwrites at the cost of slightly slower startup.

c-lang.title: 67. How does the ELF linker resolve Strong vs Weak symbols and `-fno-common` tentative definitions?
c-lang.content: Initialized globals and functions are Strong symbols, while uninitialized globals (historically `COMMON`) or `__attribute__((weak))` declarations are Weak; the linker rejects duplicate strong symbols, picks a strong symbol over weak ones, and since GCC 10 (`-fno-common`) treats uninitialized globals as strong definitions.

blocks.text:
• **Unix Linker Rules**:
  1. Multiple **strong** symbols with the same name -> Linker error (`multiple definition of ...`).
  2. One **strong** symbol and one or more **weak** symbols -> Linker silently chooses the strong symbol.
  3. Multiple **weak** symbols -> Linker picks one (or the largest `COMMON` block).
• **Why Weak Symbols Exist**: Embedded HALs and `libc` define default interrupt handlers or hooks (e.g., `__attribute__((weak)) void SysTick_Handler(void)`) that user application code can override simply by defining a strong function of the same name.
• **The `-fno-common` Shift**: Before GCC 10, forgetting `extern` in a header (`int global_flag;`) created tentative `COMMON` symbols that silently merged across `.o` files; `-fno-common` now puts them in `.bss` as strong definitions, catching accidental aliasing at link time.

c-lang.title: 68. What executes before `main()` and after `return 0` in a standard C program on Linux?
c-lang.content: The ELF entry point is `_start` (from `crt1.o`), which aligns the stack, extracts `argc`/`argv`/`envp` pushed by the kernel, and calls `__libc_start_main()` to initialize TLS, run `.preinit_array` and `.init_array` constructors, invoke `main()`, and pass its return value to `exit()`.

blocks.text:
• **Kernel `execve()` Hand-off**: The kernel maps the ELF segments, maps the dynamic linker (`ld-linux.so`), pushes `argc`, `argv` pointers, `envp` pointers, and the **ELF Auxiliary Vector (`auxv`)** onto the top of the user stack, and jumps to `_start`.
• **C Runtime (`crt1.o`, `crti.o`, `crtn.o`)**: `_start` clears `%rbp` (marking the outermost stack frame), sets up arguments, and invokes `__libc_start_main`.
• **Constructors & Destructors**: Before `main()`, `__libc_start_main` runs functions registered in `.init_array` (including `__attribute__((constructor))`). After `main()` returns, `exit()` runs `atexit()` handlers and `.fini_array` (`__attribute__((destructor))`), flushes `stdio` buffers, and invokes the `exit_group` syscall.

c-lang.title: 69. How do ELF Symbol Interposition (`LD_PRELOAD`) and `-fvisibility=hidden` affect dynamic library performance and hooking?
c-lang.content: By default, ELF exports all global symbols as `STV_DEFAULT` (preemptible), enabling `LD_PRELOAD` to intercept calls like `malloc`, whereas compiling shared libraries with `-fvisibility=hidden` hides internal functions, removes PLT/GOT overhead, and enables aggressive inlining.

blocks.text:
• **ELF Global Symbol Interposition**: When `ld-linux.so` resolves a symbol, it searches loaded objects in breadth-first order starting from the executable and any `LD_PRELOAD` libraries before `libc.so`. That allows profilers (`jemalloc`, `asan`) to override `malloc`/`free` transparently.
• **The Hidden Cost of Default Visibility**: Because any public function in a `.so` might be interposed at runtime, the compiler cannot inline intra-library calls to global functions and must route them through the `.plt`!
• **Best Practice (`-fvisibility=hidden`)**: Compile `.so` libraries with `-fvisibility=hidden` and explicitly annotate only the public ABI functions with `__attribute__((visibility("default")))`.

c-lang.title: 70. Describe the x86-64 System V ABI Stack Frame layout, register calling convention, and 16-byte stack alignment rule.
c-lang.content: Under the System V AMD64 ABI, the first 6 integer/pointer arguments pass in `RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9` (floats in `XMM0-XMM7`), return values go in `RAX`/`RDX`, callee-saved registers (`RBX, RBP, R12-R15`) must be preserved, and `RSP` must be 16-byte aligned before any `CALL` instruction.

blocks.text:
• **Frame Layout (High to Low Memory)**:
  1. Caller arguments 7+ pushed right-to-left on stack.
  2. **Return Address** (8 bytes pushed by `CALL`, which shifts `RSP` from 16-byte aligned to `16n - 8`).
  3. **Saved `RBP`** (`push rbp; mov rbp, rsp` restores 16-byte alignment of `RSP`).
  4. Saved callee-saved registers & local variables (`[rbp - offset]`).
• **Why 16-Byte Alignment Matters**: SSE/AVX instructions (e.g., `movaps`) used by `printf` or compiler auto-vectorization fault with `SIGSEGV` if the stack pointer is misaligned.
• **`-fomit-frame-pointer`**: At `-O2`, compilers omit `RBP` framing and index locals directly off `RSP`, freeing `RBP` as a general-purpose register (at the expense of simple frame-pointer stack unwinding).

c-lang.title: 71. What is the 128-byte Stack Red Zone in the x86-64 System V ABI, and why must OS kernels compile with `-mno-red-zone`?
c-lang.content: The Red Zone is a 128-byte scratch area immediately below `RSP` (`[RSP - 128, RSP)`) guaranteed by the user-space ABI not to be clobbered by POSIX signals, allowing leaf functions to allocate locals without adjusting `RSP`; kernel code must disable it because hardware interrupts use the current kernel `RSP` directly.

blocks.text:
• **Leaf Function Optimization**: A leaf function (one that calls no other functions) can store up to 128 bytes of local variables at negative offsets from `RSP` (e.g., `mov [rsp - 8], rdi`) without executing `sub rsp, N` in the prologue or `add rsp, N` in the epilogue—saving two instructions per call.
• **User-Space Guarantee**: When a POSIX signal arrives, the Linux kernel switches from user `RSP` to kernel stack (or respects the 128-byte offset on the user stack when delivering the signal frame).
• **Why Kernel Mode Breaks**: If an interrupt or exception occurs while the CPU is already in Ring 0 (kernel mode), the hardware CPU pushes `SS, RSP, RFLAGS, CS, RIP` directly at the current `RSP`, instantly overwriting any data inside the Red Zone! Hence Linux kernel Makefiles always pass `-mno-red-zone`.

c-lang.title: 72. How does the CPU actually return a `struct` by value in C when it exceeds register size?
c-lang.content: Structs up to 16 bytes (on x86-64 System V) are packed directly into return registers `RAX` and `RDX`; for structs larger than 16 bytes, the compiler allocates space in the caller's stack frame and silently passes its address as a hidden first parameter in `RDI` (`sret`).

blocks.text:
• **Small Structs (<= 16 bytes)**: Returned purely in registers (`RAX` + `RDX` or `XMM0` + `XMM1`) with zero memory copy overhead!
• **Large Structs (> 16 bytes)**: The ABI specifies an invisible pointer transformation:
  - A function declared as `BigStruct make_big(int x);` is compiled as if written `void make_big(BigStruct *hidden_sret, int x);`.
  - The caller reserves `sizeof(BigStruct)` on its stack, passes that address in `RDI`, shifts `x` to `RSI`, and the callee writes directly into the caller's memory—eliminating any intermediate copy.

c-lang.title: 73. How do Stack Canaries (`-fstack-protector-strong`), the NX bit, ASLR, and PIE work together to mitigate stack buffer overflows?
c-lang.content: Stack Canaries detect return-address corruption before `RET` executes, the hardware NX (No-Execute) bit prevents executing shellcode injected on the stack/heap, and ASLR + PIE randomize code and stack addresses to defeat Return-Oriented Programming (ROP).

blocks.text:
• **Stack Canary (`%fs:0x28`)**: The prologue copies a random 64-bit secret (ending in `0x00` to block string functions) from Thread-Local Storage (`%fs:0x28`) onto the stack right above the saved `RBP`. Before `RET`, the epilogue XORs it with `%fs:0x28` and calls `__stack_chk_fail()` if modified.
• **NX / DEP (Page Table Bit 63)**: Marks stack and heap pages non-executable in hardware page tables; jumping to stack shellcode raises `SIGSEGV`.
• **ASLR + PIE (`-fPIE -pie`)**: Kernel ASLR randomizes stack, heap, and shared library bases, but the main executable is only randomized if compiled as a **Position-Independent Executable (PIE)**.

c-lang.title: 74. How does `glibc` `ptmalloc2` structure heap chunk headers, boundary tags, and the `P`/`M`/`A` status bits?
c-lang.content: Every allocated heap chunk is preceded by an 8-byte `mchunk_size` header whose lowest 3 bits (unused due to 16-byte alignment) encode `A` (NON_MAIN_ARENA), `M` (IS_MMAPPED), and `P` (PREV_INUSE), while free chunks store forward/backward freelist pointers and a trailing boundary tag inside the unused payload.

blocks.text:
• **Zero-Overhead Bit Packing**: On 64-bit Linux, `malloc` aligns pointers to 16 bytes, so the lower 4 bits of chunk sizes are always zero. `ptmalloc2` packs 3 flags into the `size` field:
  - **Bit 0 (`P` - `PREV_INUSE`)**: Set if the physically preceding chunk is allocated. When set, the previous chunk needs no trailing size footer (saving 8 bytes per allocation!).
  - **Bit 1 (`M` - `IS_MMAPPED`)**: Chunk was allocated via standalone `mmap()`, not from an arena.
  - **Bit 2 (`A` - `NON_MAIN_ARENA`)**: Chunk belongs to a secondary thread arena.
• **O(1) Coalescing via Boundary Tags**: When `free(p)` runs, it checks bit `P` of the current chunk header. If `P == 0`, it reads `prev_size` (the boundary tag at the end of the previous free chunk) to jump backward in $O(1)$ and merge adjacent free chunks into one larger chunk.

c-lang.title: 75. Explain `glibc` `malloc` arenas, per-thread `tcache`, and the hierarchy of `fastbins`, `unsorted`, `small`, and `large` bins.
c-lang.content: To avoid global lock contention, `glibc` uses per-thread `tcache` (lockless LIFO up to 1032 bytes, 7 chunks per size) and multiple thread arenas, each categorizing freed chunks into singly-linked `fastbins` (no coalescing) and doubly-linked `unsorted`, `small` (exact size), and `large` (best-fit) bins.

blocks.text:
• **1. `tcache` (Thread Local Cache, glibc 2.26+)**: Checked first with **zero mutex locks**. Holds up to 7 freed chunks per size class (24B to 1032B on 64-bit). If hit, `malloc`/`free` takes just a few CPU cycles.
• **2. Arenas**: Up to `8 * CPU_CORES` independent heaps, each guarded by its own mutex (`ar_ptr->mutex`) to reduce multithreaded lock contention.
• **3. Bin Hierarchy (inside an Arena)**:
  - **`fastbins`**: Singly-linked LIFO for small chunks (<= 160B); keeps `PREV_INUSE=1` to skip coalescing for speed.
  - **`unsorted bin`**: Recently freed/coalesced chunks get one quick recycling chance before sorting.
  - **`small bins`**: 62 exact-size FIFO doubly-linked lists (< 1024B, $O(1)$ lookup).
  - **`large bins`**: 63 skip-list/sorted ranges (>= 1024B, best-fit lookup).

c-lang.title: 76. When does `malloc()` use `brk()`/`sbrk()` versus `mmap()`, and why doesn't `free()` always return memory to the OS?
c-lang.content: Small allocations grow the main arena's contiguous heap via `brk()` and stay cached in bins after `free()` unless the top-of-heap wilderness chunk exceeds `M_TRIM_THRESHOLD`, whereas allocations `>= M_MMAP_THRESHOLD` (default 128KB, dynamically adjusted up to 32MB) use standalone anonymous `mmap()` regions that `munmap()` returns to the OS immediately on `free()`.

blocks.text:
• **`brk()` / Top Chunk Pinning**: The main arena expands a single contiguous data segment upward via `brk()`. If you allocate 1,000 chunks of 64KB, free the first 999, but keep the **last** chunk at the highest address alive, `brk()` cannot shrink downward—pinning the entire 64MB in the process's RSS!
• **`mmap()` Threshold**: Requests `>= 128KB` (tunable via `mallopt(M_MMAP_THRESHOLD, bytes)`) get a private anonymous VMA via `mmap(NULL, size, PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE, MAP_PRIVATE|MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0)`. Calling `free()` immediately executes `munmap()`, releasing physical pages back to the kernel.
• **`malloc_trim(0)`**: Walks arenas and calls `madvise(MADV_DONTNEED)` / `sbrk(-n)` to release free tail/interior pages back to the OS.

c-lang.title: 77. Why do high-performance C systems (compilers, game engines, databases) replace `malloc`/`free` with Arena (Bump) and Slab/Pool Allocators?
c-lang.content: General-purpose `malloc` incurs metadata overhead, lock/bin lookup latency, and heap fragmentation; an Arena (Bump) Allocator reduces allocation to a single pointer addition (`ptr += aligned_size`) and frees thousands of objects in $O(1)$ by resetting one offset.

blocks.text:
• **Arena / Linear Bump Allocator**: Pre-reserves a large contiguous block (or `mmap` virtual range). Allocation simply advances an offset: `void *p = base + offset; offset += align16(size);`. Individual `free()` is a no-op; the entire request/frame lifecycle is freed at once via `arena->offset = 0` in $O(1)$ with superior cache locality.
• **Fixed-Size Pool / Slab Allocator**: Divides a page into fixed-size slots embedding an intrusive singly-linked free-list inside the unallocated slots themselves. Both `pool_alloc()` and `pool_free()` execute in $O(1)$ (2 pointer assignments) with zero external fragmentation.

c-lang.title: 78. How does `glibc` 2.32+ Safe-Linking (`PROTECT_PTR`) defend `tcache` and `fastbin` freelist pointers against heap exploitation?
c-lang.content: Safe-Linking XORs every singly-linked `fd` pointer in `tcache` and `fastbins` with the ASLR-randomized address of the pointer slot itself shifted right by 12 bits (`(&fd >> 12) ^ target`), preventing attackers from hijacking freelist pointers without an address leak and enforcing 16-byte alignment checks.

blocks.text:
• **Classic `tcache` Poisoning**: Before glibc 2.32, a free chunk stored its next pointer `fd` in plaintext inside the first 8 bytes of the freed payload. A Use-After-Free write could overwrite `fd` with any target address, and the second `malloc()` would return that arbitrary pointer.
• **Safe-Linking Mechanism**:
  - Encode on `free()`: `chunk->fd = ((uintptr_t)&chunk->fd >> 12) ^ (uintptr_t)next_chunk;`
  - Decode on `malloc()`: `next_chunk = ((uintptr_t)&chunk->fd >> 12) ^ chunk->fd;`
• **Integrity Validation**: On decode, `glibc` verifies `(uintptr_t)next_chunk & 0xF == 0` (16-byte aligned); if corrupted, it aborts with `malloc(): unaligned tcache chunk detected`.

c-lang.title: 79. How does Type-Based Alias Analysis (TBAA) exploit the Strict Aliasing Rule at `-O2` to hoist loads and break naive pointer casts?
c-lang.content: Under C11 §6.5p7 (Strict Aliasing), pointers to distinct types (like `uint32_t *` and `uint16_t *`) cannot alias the same memory object, enabling the `-O2` optimizer to reorder stores after loads or cache values in registers across writes through incompatible pointers.

blocks.text:
• **The Effective Type Rule**: An object's effective type is set by its declaration or (for heap memory with no declared type) by the type of the first non-character lvalue write. Reading it via an incompatible type is UB.
• **Why Code Breaks Only at `-O2`**: At `-O0`, every pointer read/write goes to stack memory. At `-O2` (`-fstrict-aliasing`), TBAA proves that writing to `*u16_ptr` cannot legally modify `*u32_ptr`, so the compiler hoists or eliminates the reload of `*u32_ptr`!
• **Sanctioned Escapes**:
  1. `memcpy(&dst, &src, sizeof(dst))` (always valid, compiles to a single register move).
  2. Inspecting bytes via `unsigned char *` or `char *` (cannot alias the reverse way!).
  3. GCC/Clang `__attribute__((__may_alias__))` on typedefs.

c-lang.title: 80. Why does the compiler optimize away `memset(secret_key, 0, sizeof(secret_key))` before a function returns, and how do you prevent it?
c-lang.content: Dead Store Elimination (DSE) removes writes to local stack buffers that are never read again before going out of scope, leaving cryptographic secrets exposed on the stack; prevent this using C23 `memset_explicit()`, POSIX `explicit_bzero()`, C11 `memset_s()`, or a compiler memory barrier.

blocks.text:
• **The Security Vulnerability**: Under the C abstract machine's "as-if" rule, writing zeros to a local array right before `return` (or right before `free(ptr)` with Link-Time Optimization) has no observable side effect in valid C, so `-O2` deletes the entire `memset()` call!
• **Why secret leakage matters**: Subsequent function calls reuse that same stack memory or core dumps/heartbleed-style bugs can read residual stack/heap bytes.
• **Portable Fixes**:
  - **C23 Standard**: `memset_explicit(key, 0, sizeof(key))`
  - **glibc / BSD**: `explicit_bzero(key, sizeof(key))`
  - **Inline Assembly Barrier**: `__asm__ __volatile__("" : : "r"(buf) : "memory");` forces the compiler to assume `buf` is observed externally.

c-lang.title: 81. How can dereferencing a pointer before a `if (ptr == NULL)` check cause the compiler to delete the NULL check entirely?
c-lang.content: Because dereferencing a `NULL` pointer is Undefined Behavior in C, the compiler deduces that after `*ptr` is evaluated on any code path, `ptr` can never be `NULL`—and consequently deletes any subsequent `if (!ptr)` defensive check as dead code.

blocks.text:
• **Time-Travel UB Optimization**: Look at `int x = ptr->field; if (!ptr) return -EINVAL;`. Even if `x` is never used before the `if`, the mere act of evaluating `ptr->field` executes a load from `ptr`.
• **Compiler Reasoning**:
  1. In valid C, a dereferenced pointer cannot be `NULL`.
  2. Since `ptr` was just dereferenced on line 1, `ptr != NULL` is now a proven invariant.
  3. Therefore, `if (!ptr)` on line 2 is provably `false` and gets stripped out at `-O2`!
• **Real-World Impact (CVE-2009-1897)**: This exact optimization deleted a NULL check in the Linux kernel's `tun_chr_poll()` driver; when page zero was mapped, it led to a full Ring-0 privilege escalation exploit.

c-lang.title: 82. What is Pointer Provenance in modern C compilers, and what are the rules for the 'one-past-the-end' pointer (`&arr[N]`)?
c-lang.content: C allows forming and comparing a pointer one element past the end of an array (`arr + N`) without dereferencing it, but Pointer Provenance tracks which underlying object a pointer was derived from—making it UB to use `arr1 + N` to read/write an adjacent variable `arr2` even if their numeric addresses are identical.

blocks.text:
• **One-Past-The-End (`&arr[N]`)**: Strictly legal to compute and compare in loop bounds (`for (int *p = a; p < a + N; ++p)`). Computing `a + N + 1` or `a - 1` (before index 0), or dereferencing `*(a + N)`, is immediate Undefined Behavior.
• **Pointer Provenance**: Compilers do not treat pointers as raw 64-bit integers. A pointer carries hidden compile-time metadata (provenance) binding it to its original allocation object.
• **Why `p == q` Doesn't Mean Interchangeable**: If `int a[4], b[4];` sit adjacent in memory so `(uintptr_t)(a + 4) == (uintptr_t)b`, comparing `(a + 4) == b` may fold to `true`, yet writing `*(a + 4) = 42` is UB because `a + 4` has provenance of `a` (at end boundary) and cannot legally mutate `b`!

c-lang.title: 83. Why is reading an uninitialized local variable Undefined Behavior in C rather than just returning a 'random garbage value'?
c-lang.content: An uninitialized automatic variable whose address is never taken holds an indeterminate value (represented as `poison`/`undef` in LLVM/GCC IR), allowing the optimizer to evaluate `bool b; if (b)` and `if (!b)` as simultaneously false or eliminate entire branches.

blocks.text:
• **Not Just Stack Garbage**: Many developers assume an uninitialized `int x;` simply holds whatever bits were left on the stack and stays consistent if read twice (`x == x` is always true). In optimizing compilers, that assumption is **false**!
• **C Standard Rule (C11 §6.3.2.1p2)**: If an automatic variable has an indeterminate value and **never has its address taken** (meaning it is eligible for the `register` storage class), reading it is immediate Undefined Behavior.
• **LLVM `undef` / `poison` Semantics**: Since the variable isn't bound to a stack slot yet, the compiler can pick a different value on each read or optimize away any branch that depends on it (breaking naive "entropy harvesting" code like Debian OpenSSL's infamous RNG bug).

c-lang.title: 84. Why is casting an unaligned `uint8_t *` buffer to `uint32_t *` Undefined Behavior even on x86-64 CPUs that support unaligned loads?
c-lang.content: Forming or dereferencing a misaligned pointer violates C11 §6.3.2.3p7; even on x86-64, `-O2` auto-vectorization emits aligned SIMD instructions (`movdqa`/`vmovaps`) that fault with `SIGBUS`/`SIGSEGV` on unaligned addresses—use `memcpy()` for zero-overhead unaligned reads.

blocks.text:
• **The "x86 Allows Unaligned Loads" Myth**: While scalar x86 `mov eax, [rdi]` tolerates unaligned addresses, the C compiler assumes every `uint32_t *` is 4-byte aligned and every `uint64_t *` is 8-byte aligned.
• **Why It Crashes on x86-64 at `-O2`/`-O3`**: When the compiler vectorizes a loop over `uint32_t *` or optimizes adjacent struct assignments, it emits aligned SSE instructions that require 16-byte alignment and crash immediately if the pointer came from an arbitrary byte offset in a network packet buffer! On ARMv7/MIPS, even scalar `LDRD` faults with `SIGBUS`.
• **The Optimal Solution (`memcpy`)**: `uint32_t v; memcpy(&v, buf + offset, sizeof(v));` compiles down to a single unaligned `mov eax, DWORD PTR [rdi+offset]` on x86-64 with zero function-call overhead and 100% standard compliance.

c-lang.title: 85. What is the C11 Forward Progress Guarantee, and when can a compiler delete or fall through an infinite loop?
c-lang.content: Under C11 §6.8.5p6, the compiler may assume that any loop whose controlling expression is NOT a constant expression eventually terminates if it performs no I/O, volatile accesses, or atomic/synchronization operations—whereas `while (1)` or `for (;;)` with a constant controlling expression is explicitly exempt in C.

blocks.text:
• **C11 §6.8.5p6 Rule**: An iteration statement whose controlling expression is **not a constant expression**, and that performs no input/output operations, does not access `volatile` objects, and performs no synchronization or atomic operations, may be assumed by the implementation to terminate.
• **Important C vs C++ Difference**:
  - In C11/C17/C23, `while (1) {}` or `for (;;) {}` has a **constant** controlling expression, so the C standard requires it to spin forever even if the body is empty!
  - However, if the condition is a non-constant variable computation (e.g., `while (collatz(n) != 1) {}` with no side effects), the C compiler can assume it terminates and optimize away the loop.

c-lang.title: 86. How do 64-byte CPU Cache Lines, the MESI coherency protocol, Store Buffers, and Invalidation Queues affect multithreaded C?
c-lang.content: CPU cores exchange memory in 64-byte cache lines tracked via MESI states (Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid); to avoid stalling on cache-coherency handshakes, cores queue writes in private Store Buffers and queue incoming invalidations, which causes memory reordering across threads without memory barriers.

blocks.text:
• **MESI Protocol States**:
  - **Modified (M)**: Present only in this core's cache, dirty (must be written back before another core reads).
  - **Exclusive (E)**: Present only in this core's cache, clean (matches RAM).
  - **Shared (S)**: Replicated clean across multiple cores.
  - **Invalid (I)**: Line is stale and cannot be read.
• **Why Memory Reordering Happens in Hardware**: When Core 0 writes to a `Shared` line, it must send an `Invalidate` message to Core 1 and wait for an `Invalidate Acknowledge`. Instead of stalling the pipeline for dozens of cycles, Core 0 drops the write into its private **Store Buffer** and immediately executes subsequent loads from other cache lines—making Core 0's loads appear to execute *before* its earlier store to other cores!

c-lang.title: 87. When and how should you use `__builtin_prefetch()` and `__builtin_expect()` (`likely`/`unlikely`) in performance-critical C?
c-lang.content: `__builtin_prefetch(addr, rw, locality)` hides ~60ns RAM latency by loading a cache line ahead of pointer-chasing or non-linear lookups where hardware stream prefetchers fail, while `__builtin_expect(expr, 1)` guides compiler basic-block layout to keep the hot path fall-through and instruction-cache dense.

blocks.text:
